cards.front: Identical conducting spheres A and B have +8 nC and −2 nC. They touch and separate. B then touches an identical neutral sphere C. Find the final charge on each and check total charge conservation.
cards.back: Initially the total is +6 nC. After A and B touch, each has +3 nC. B and neutral C then share B’s +3 nC equally, so B = +1.5 nC and C = +1.5 nC. A remains +3 nC. Final total = 3 + 1.5 + 1.5 = +6 nC.

cards.front: An initially neutral object ends with charge +6.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Determine how many electrons were transferred and in which direction. Explain why a nearby neutral conductor can still be attracted to it without touching.
cards.back: n = |Q|/e = (6.4 × 10⁻¹⁹)/(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 4. Four electrons left the object. A nearby conductor can polarise: electrons shift toward the positive object, placing opposite charge closer than like charge. The attraction can dominate while the conductor’s total charge remains zero.

cards.front: What moves in ordinary charging of solid objects: protons or electrons?
cards.back: Electrons move; protons normally remain bound in nuclei.

cards.front: What does a negative net charge indicate?
cards.back: An excess of electrons compared with the neutral state.

cards.front: What direction do external magnetic field lines take around a bar magnet?
cards.back: From the north pole to the south pole outside the magnet.

cards.front: What does a denser pattern of magnetic field lines represent?
cards.back: A stronger magnetic field in the diagram’s model.

cards.front: Why can a charged object attract a neutral object even though the neutral object has no net charge?
cards.back: The charged object can redistribute charges or polarise the neutral material. Opposite charge is brought closer than like charge, making the attraction stronger than the repulsion. Net neutrality does not mean charges cannot respond.

cards.front: A bar magnet is cut in half. Why do the pieces not become separate north-only and south-only magnets?
cards.back: Each piece retains aligned magnetic domains and has its own north and south poles. Cutting changes the size and arrangement, but it does not isolate a single magnetic pole in this model.

topics.subject: physical
topics.title: Electric circuits

notes.heading: What are current, voltage and resistance?
notes.body: Current is charge flow per unit time. Potential difference is energy transferred per unit charge. Resistance is the ratio V/I for a component at the stated operating conditions.

notes.heading: How do series circuits combine?
notes.body: Current is the same through series components. Resistances add and the supply voltage is shared. An ammeter is connected in series.

notes.heading: How do parallel circuits combine?
notes.body: Parallel branches share the same potential difference. Branch currents add at a junction. For resistors, reciprocals of resistance add. A voltmeter is connected across a component.

practice.question: A 12 V battery is connected across a 6 Ω resistor. Find the current and charge passing in 30 s.
Find the total resistance of 6 Ω and 3 Ω connected in parallel.
practice.answer: 1/R = 1/6 + 1/3 = 3/6 = 1/2, so R = 2 Ω. It is smaller than either individual resistance.

practice.question: Resistors of 4 Ω and 8 Ω are connected in series to a 6 V supply. Find total resistance and current.
practice.answer: Series resistances add: R = 4 + 8 = 12 Ω. I = V/R = 6/12 = 0.5 A, the same current through both resistors.

practice.question: Two 12 Ω resistors are connected in parallel across a 6 V supply. Find total resistance and total current.
practice.answer: 1/R = 1/12 + 1/12 = 1/6, so R = 6 Ω. Total current = V/R = 6/6 = 1 A. Each branch carries 6/12 = 0.5 A.

practice.question: A current of 0.4 A flows for 2 minutes. Calculate the charge passing a point.
practice.answer: Convert time to seconds: t = 2 × 60 = 120 s. Q = It = 0.4 × 120 = 48 C.

practice.question: A resistor carries 0.3 A when the potential difference is 9 V. Calculate its resistance and the current at 6 V, assuming constant resistance.
practice.answer: R = V/I = 9/0.3 = 30 Ω. At 6 V, I = 6/30 = 0.2 A. This assumes conditions such as temperature keep the resistance unchanged.

topics.tip: Show your reasoning and check the units or restrictions in your final answer.

challenges.question: A second resistor is added in parallel to a resistor across an ideal battery. Explain why the total battery current increases while the original branch current stays the same.
challenges.answer: The extra branch gives another conducting path and reduces equivalent resistance. An ideal battery maintains the same potential difference across each branch. The original branch resistance and voltage are unchanged, so its current remains V/R; total current is the sum of the branch currents.

challenges.question: A learner says a resistor “uses up current”. Explain why this is misleading in a steady series circuit.
challenges.answer: Charge is conserved, so the current entering and leaving a resistor is the same in steady operation. The resistor transfers electrical energy to other forms, often thermal energy. Energy is transferred; charge is not consumed.

cards.front: A 4 Ω resistor is in series with a parallel combination of 6 Ω and 3 Ω. The supply is 12 V. Find total current, voltage across the parallel part, and current through each branch.
cards.back: Parallel resistance: 1/Rp = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2, so Rp = 2 Ω. Total R = 4 + 2 = 6 Ω and total I = 12/6 = 2 A. Series resistor drop = 2 × 4 = 8 V, leaving 4 V across each parallel branch. Branch currents are 4/6 = 2/3 A and 4/3 A; they add to 2 A.

cards.front: Two equal resistors are connected in parallel across a 9 V battery. The total current is 3 A. Find each resistor’s resistance and the charge through one branch in 2 minutes.
cards.back: Equivalent resistance = 9/3 = 3 Ω. For two equal parallel resistors, each R = 2 × 3 = 6 Ω. Each branch current = 9/6 = 1.5 A. Convert 2 min to 120 s: branch charge Q = It = 1.5 × 120 = 180 C.

cards.front: What is shared equally across parallel branches?
cards.back: Potential difference; branch currents need not be equal.

cards.front: Where is an ammeter connected?
cards.back: In series with the current being measured.

cards.front: Where is a voltmeter connected?
cards.back: Across the component, in parallel.

cards.front: What is the unit of electric charge?
cards.back: The coulomb (C); Q = It when current is constant.

topics.subject: physical
topics.title: Vectors & motion graphs

notes.heading: What makes a quantity a vector?
notes.body: A vector has both magnitude and direction. Displacement, velocity and force are vectors; distance, speed and energy are scalars. Choose a positive direction before calculating.

notes.heading: How do you add perpendicular vectors?
notes.body: Draw a head-to-tail diagram. Use Pythagoras for the resultant magnitude and trigonometry for its direction. The equilibrant has equal magnitude and opposite direction.

notes.heading: How do you read motion graphs?
notes.body: Gradient of displacement-time gives velocity. Gradient of velocity-time gives acceleration. Signed area under velocity-time gives displacement; add absolute areas for distance.

notes.heading: Translate the representation before calculating
notes.body: A vector needs magnitude and direction. On a position–time graph, gradient gives velocity; on a velocity–time graph, gradient gives acceleration and signed area gives displacement. Area below the time axis is negative displacement. Distance requires adding the magnitudes of the separate displacement areas.

practice.question: Forces of 6 N east and 8 N north act together. Find the resultant.
practice.answer: Magnitude = √(6² + 8²) = 10 N. Direction θ = tan⁻¹(8/6) = 53.13° north of east.

practice.question: A velocity-time graph rises uniformly from 0 to 12 m/s in 4 s. Find acceleration and displacement.
practice.answer: a = (12 − 0)/4 = 3 m/s². Displacement is the triangular area: ½ × 4 × 12 = 24 m in the positive direction.

practice.question: A learner walks 5 m east and then 2 m west. Find the total distance and displacement.
practice.answer: Distance adds path lengths: 5 + 2 = 7 m. Taking east positive, displacement = 5 − 2 = 3 m east.

practice.question: A car changes velocity uniformly from 4 m/s east to 16 m/s east in 6 s. Find its acceleration.
practice.answer: Take east as positive. a = (v − u)/t = (16 − 4)/6 = 2 m/s² east.

practice.question: An object moves with constant velocity −3 m/s for 4 s. Find its displacement and distance travelled.
practice.answer: Signed area under the velocity-time graph gives displacement: (−3)(4) = −12 m. The distance is the magnitude of the path in this interval: 12 m.

practice.question: Forces of 9 N east and 12 N north act together. State the magnitude of the resultant and of the equilibrant.
practice.answer: The forces are perpendicular. Resultant magnitude = √(9² + 12²) = √225 = 15 N. The equilibrant also has magnitude 15 N but points exactly opposite to the resultant.

topics.tip: Show your reasoning and check the units or restrictions in your final answer.

challenges.question: Can an object have zero velocity and non-zero acceleration at the same instant? Explain with a physical example.
challenges.answer: Yes. A ball thrown vertically upward has zero instantaneous velocity at its highest point, while gravity still accelerates it downward. Velocity describes motion at an instant; acceleration describes how velocity is changing.

challenges.question: A velocity–time graph lies below the time axis but slopes upward. Is the object speeding up? Explain using direction and magnitude.
challenges.answer: Its velocity is negative and becoming less negative, so the speed, the magnitude of velocity, is decreasing until it reaches zero. Positive acceleration does not always mean increasing speed; the velocity direction matters.

cards.front: A velocity-time graph rises linearly from 0 to 8 m/s in 4 s, stays at 8 m/s for 3 s, then falls linearly to −4 m/s over 6 s. Find total displacement, distance and average velocity over all 13 s.
cards.back: First area = ½(4)(8) = 16 m; constant section = 3(8) = 24 m. Final acceleration is (−4 − 8)/6 = −2 m/s², so velocity reaches zero after 4 s of that section. Its positive area is ½(4)(8) = 16 m and negative area is −½(2)(4) = −4 m. Displacement = 16 + 24 + 16 − 4 = 52 m. Distance = 16 + 24 + 16 + 4 = 60 m. Average velocity = 52/13 = 4 m/s in the positive direction.

cards.front: An object travels 12 m north, then 5 m east in 10 s total. Find average speed and average velocity, giving a direction for the latter.
cards.back: Distance = 12 + 5 = 17 m, so average speed = 1.7 m/s. Displacement magnitude = √(12² + 5²) = 13 m. Average velocity magnitude = 13/10 = 1.3 m/s, at tan⁻¹(5/12) ≈ 22.62° east of north.

cards.front: What does signed area under a velocity-time graph give?
cards.back: Displacement.

cards.front: How do you get distance from a velocity-time graph?
cards.back: Add the absolute areas above and below the time axis.

cards.front: Can negative velocity occur with positive acceleration?
cards.back: Yes. The object can move in the negative direction while slowing down.

cards.front: What is an equilibrant relative to a resultant?
cards.back: A vector of equal magnitude and opposite direction.

topics.subject: physical
topics.title: Energy & conservation

notes.heading: Where is mechanical energy stored?
notes.body: Kinetic energy is associated with motion. Gravitational potential energy depends on mass, field strength and height relative to a chosen reference level.

notes.heading: When is mechanical energy conserved?
notes.body: If only conservative forces do work, total kinetic plus potential energy stays constant. With friction, mechanical energy can become thermal energy, while total energy is still conserved.

notes.heading: How does speed affect kinetic energy?
notes.body: Kinetic energy depends on speed squared. Doubling speed at constant mass quadruples kinetic energy. Always convert grams to kilograms and use metres and seconds.

topics.formula: Eₖ = ½mv²  •  Eₚ = mgh  •  g = 9.8 m/s²

practice.question: A 2 kg object moves at 3 m/s. Find its kinetic energy.
An object falls from rest through 5 m with no air resistance. Find its speed just before reaching the bottom.
practice.answer: mgh = ½mv², so v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.8 × 5) = √98 ≈ 9.90 m/s downward.

practice.question: A 5 kg object is 2 m above a reference level. Calculate its gravitational potential energy with g = 9.8 m/s².
practice.answer: Eₚ = mgh = 5 × 9.8 × 2 = 98 J relative to the stated level.

practice.question: A 4 kg ball has kinetic energy 50 J. Calculate its speed.
practice.answer: Eₖ = ½mv² gives 50 = ½(4)v² = 2v². Thus v² = 25 and speed v = 5 m/s.

practice.question: An object’s speed triples while its mass stays constant. By what factor does its kinetic energy change?
practice.answer: Eₖ depends on v². Replacing v by 3v gives (3v)² = 9v², so kinetic energy becomes 9 times the original value.

practice.question: A system starts with 200 J of mechanical energy and loses 35 J of mechanical energy to friction. Find its final mechanical energy and explain what happened to the missing amount.
practice.answer: Final mechanical energy = 200 − 35 = 165 J. The 35 J was transferred mainly into thermal energy, so total energy is conserved even though mechanical energy is reduced.

topics.tip: Show your reasoning and check the units or restrictions in your final answer.

challenges.question: Two balls of different masses fall through the same height with air resistance neglected. Explain why they reach the same speed although their kinetic energies differ.
challenges.answer: mgh = ½mv², so mass cancels when finding speed. Both reach √(2gh) from rest. The heavier ball has greater kinetic energy at that speed because kinetic energy is proportional to mass.

challenges.question: A sliding object slows because of friction. Is this a failure of energy conservation? Explain the system boundary.
challenges.answer: No. The object’s mechanical energy decreases while thermal energy of the surfaces and surroundings increases. Mechanical energy is not conserved in this process, but total energy is conserved when the system includes the relevant surroundings.

cards.front: A 2 kg object starts from rest 5 m above the ground. It loses 18 J of mechanical energy to friction before reaching the ground. Find its speed there, using g = 9.8 m/s².
cards.back: Initial Eₚ = mgh = 2 × 9.8 × 5 = 98 J. Final kinetic energy = 98 − 18 = 80 J. Since Eₖ = ½(2)v² = v², v = √80 = 4√5 ≈ 8.94 m/s. Mechanical energy decreases, while total energy including thermal transfers is conserved.

cards.front: Object A has mass m and speed v. Object B has half A’s mass. Find B’s speed if it must have the same kinetic energy as A. Then compare B’s energy with A’s if it instead moves at 2v.
cards.back: Equal energy requires ½(m/2)u² = ½mv², so u² = 2v² and u = √2 v for speed. At 2v, B’s kinetic energy is ½(m/2)(2v)² = mv², which is twice A’s ½mv².

cards.front: Which quantity is squared in kinetic energy?
cards.back: Speed: Eₖ = ½mv².

cards.front: What condition permits mechanical-energy conservation?
cards.back: Only conservative forces do work on the chosen system, or non-conservative work is zero.

cards.front: Does friction destroy total energy?
cards.back: No. It transfers mechanical energy into other forms, often thermal energy.

cards.front: Why must a reference level be stated for gravitational potential energy?
cards.back: The value mgh depends on the chosen zero of height; energy differences are what matter physically.

topics.subject: physical
topics.title: Atomic structure & periodicity

notes.heading: How do you count particles?
notes.body: Atomic number Z counts protons; mass number A counts protons plus neutrons. A neutral atom has Z electrons. Ions form when electrons are lost or gained.

notes.heading: What are isotopes?
notes.body: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different neutron counts. They have the same Z but different A. Relative atomic mass is a weighted mean of isotope masses.

notes.heading: How does the periodic table help?
notes.body: For main-group elements, similar valence-electron arrangements produce similar chemical properties. Across a period, valence patterns change systematically.

topics.formula: neutrons = A − Z  •  Ar = Σ(isotope mass × fraction)

practice.question: A neutral atom has Z = 12 and A = 24. State its proton, neutron and electron numbers.
practice.answer: Protons = 12; neutrons = 24 − 12 = 12; electrons = 12. Its 2+ ion would have 10 electrons.

practice.question: An element has 75% isotope of mass 35 and 25% isotope of mass 37. Find the weighted atomic mass.
An ion has 17 protons, 18 electrons and 20 neutrons. State its atomic number, mass number and charge.
practice.answer: Atomic number Z = 17. Mass number A = protons + neutrons = 17 + 20 = 37. One extra electron gives a charge of −1, so it is Cl⁻.

practice.question: Atoms X and Y both have 8 protons. X has 8 neutrons and Y has 10. Explain whether they are isotopes.
practice.answer: They are isotopes of the same element because their proton counts are equal while their neutron counts differ. Their mass numbers are 16 and 18 respectively.

practice.question: An element has isotopes of mass 10 and 11 in abundances of 20% and 80%. Calculate its relative atomic mass.
A neutral main-group atom has electron-shell arrangement 2,8,1. State how it forms a stable positive ion and the ion’s electron arrangement.
practice.answer: It can lose its one outer electron to form a 1+ ion. The remaining electron arrangement is 2,8. The proton count does not change during ion formation.

topics.tip: Show your reasoning and check the units or restrictions in your final answer.

challenges.question: An atom becomes a positive ion. Why does it remain the same element?
challenges.answer: A positive ion forms by losing electrons. Element identity depends on proton number, which stays unchanged. Changing neutron number would change the isotope; changing proton number would change the element.

challenges.question: Why does atomic radius generally decrease across a period, even though more electrons are being added?
challenges.answer: Proton number increases while added electrons enter the same main energy level. Shielding does not increase enough to cancel the stronger nuclear attraction, so the outer electron cloud is generally drawn closer. This is a trend, not a rule without exceptions.

A neutral main-group atom has electron-shell arrangement 2,8,1. State how it forms a stable positive ion and the ion’s electron arrangement.
cards.back: It can lose its one outer electron to form a 1+ ion. The remaining electron arrangement is 2,8. The proton count does not change during ion formation.

cards.front: An element’s isotopes have masses 35 and 37. Its relative atomic mass is 35.6. Find each percentage abundance. Then state the proton, neutron and electron counts in its mass-37 ion with Z = 17 and charge −1.
cards.back: Let the mass-35 fraction be x: 35x + 37(1 − x) = 35.6. Thus 37 − 2x = 35.6, giving x = 0.7. Abundances are 70% mass-35 and 30% mass-37. For the specified ion: protons = 17, neutrons = 37 − 17 = 20, electrons = 18.

cards.front: X²⁺ and Y⁻ each have 10 electrons. Determine the atomic numbers of X and Y and explain why equal electron counts do not make them the same element.
cards.back: X²⁺ lost two electrons, so neutral X has 12 electrons and Z = 12. Y⁻ gained one, so neutral Y has 9 electrons and Z = 9. They are different elements because element identity depends on proton number, not on an ion’s electron count.

cards.front: How do you find neutrons from A and Z?
cards.back: Neutrons = A − Z.

cards.front: Does forming an ion change atomic number?
cards.back: No. Electron loss or gain does not change the proton count.

cards.front: What must isotope fractions add to?
cards.back: 1, or 100% when using percentage abundances.

cards.front: What makes two atoms isotopes of the same element?
cards.back: The same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

topics.subject: physical
topics.title: Bonding & chemical formulae

notes.heading: How do ionic and covalent bonds differ?
notes.body: Ionic bonding is electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions after electron transfer. Covalent bonding involves shared electron pairs between atoms.

notes.heading: How do you write an ionic formula?
notes.body: Balance positive and negative charges to make an electrically neutral formula unit. Reduce to the lowest whole-number ratio. Use brackets for repeated polyatomic ions.

notes.heading: What does a Lewis diagram show?
notes.body: Show valence electrons as dots or crosses, paired bonding electrons and lone pairs. Distinguish molecules from ionic lattices; a solid ionic compound is not made of separate molecules.

topics.formula: Total positive charge + total negative charge = 0

practice.question: Write the formula for the compound formed by Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻.
practice.answer: One Mg²⁺ requires two Cl⁻ ions to balance charge: MgCl₂. The net charge is +2 + 2(−1) = 0.

practice.question: How many bonding pairs and lone pairs are around oxygen in H₂O?
practice.answer: Oxygen has 6 valence electrons. It shares one pair with each of two hydrogens, giving 2 bonding pairs and leaving 2 lone pairs on oxygen.

practice.question: Write the electrically neutral formula formed by Al³⁺ and O²⁻.
practice.answer: The lowest common total charge is 6. Use two Al³⁺ ions and three O²⁻ ions: Al₂O₃. Total charge = 2(+3) + 3(−2) = 0.

practice.question: Write the formula for calcium nitrate using Ca²⁺ and NO₃⁻.
practice.answer: Two nitrate ions balance one Ca²⁺ ion. Because nitrate is a repeated polyatomic ion, write Ca(NO₃)₂.

practice.question: Explain the bonding difference between Cl₂ and NaCl.
practice.answer: In Cl₂, two chlorine atoms share a pair of electrons in a covalent bond. In NaCl, electron transfer produces Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions held together by electrostatic attraction in an ionic lattice.

practice.question: How many shared electron pairs occur in a nitrogen molecule N₂? Explain using the triple-bond notation.
practice.answer: N≡N has a triple covalent bond: three shared electron pairs, containing six shared electrons in total. Each nitrogen also has a lone pair.

topics.tip: Show your reasoning and check the units or restrictions in your final answer.

challenges.question: Why does solid sodium chloride not conduct like molten sodium chloride, even though both contain ions?
challenges.answer: In the solid, ions are held in a lattice and cannot move freely through the material. Melting permits ions to move and carry charge. Conductivity requires mobile charged particles, not merely the presence of charge.

challenges.question: A learner explains the formula MgCl₂ by saying one magnesium atom “wants two chlorine atoms”. Replace this with a charge-based explanation.
challenges.answer: Magnesium forms Mg²⁺ and chlorine forms Cl⁻. Two chloride ions balance the charge of one magnesium ion, giving an electrically neutral formula unit MgCl₂. The ratio follows charge balance, not a description of an atom’s intentions.

cards.front: How do ionic and covalent bonds differ?
cards.back: Ionic bonding is electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions after electron transfer. Covalent bonding involves shared electron pairs between atoms.

cards.back: N≡N has a triple covalent bond: three shared electron pairs, containing six shared electrons in total. Each nitrogen also has a lone pair.

cards.front: Aluminium forms Al³⁺ and sulfate is SO₄²⁻. Write the neutral compound formula and count the numbers of Al, S and O atoms represented in one formula unit.
cards.back: Charge balance requires 2 Al³⁺ ions (+6) and 3 sulfate ions (−6), so the formula is Al₂(SO₄)₃. It represents 2 Al, 3 S and 12 O atoms per formula unit. Parentheses apply the subscript 3 to the entire sulfate group.

cards.front: Compare bonding and electrical conductivity in solid NaCl, molten NaCl and a simple molecular substance such as CO₂. Explain using particles rather than only naming bond types.
cards.back: NaCl is an ionic lattice. In the solid its ions are fixed in place, so it does not conduct through freely moving ions. When molten, its ions can move and carry charge. CO₂ has covalent bonds within neutral molecules and normally lacks mobile ions or delocalised electrons, so pure CO₂ is not a typical electrical conductor.

cards.front: Why are brackets needed in Ca(NO₃)₂?
cards.back: There are two entire nitrate ions, so the subscript multiplies both N and O counts.

cards.front: What is a covalent bond?
cards.back: An electrostatic attraction involving a shared electron pair and the bonded nuclei.

cards.front: Why are ionic formulae written in lowest whole-number charge-balanced ratios?
cards.back: The compound is electrically neutral overall; the formula represents its simplest ion ratio.

cards.front: What do lone pairs represent in a Lewis diagram?
cards.back: Valence electron pairs not shared in a bond.

topics.subject: physical
topics.title: Chemical reactions & redox

notes.heading: Why must equations be balanced?
notes.body: Atoms and total charge are conserved. Change coefficients in front of formulae, never subscripts inside a chemical formula. Check every element after balancing.

notes.heading: How do you recognise redox?
notes.body: Oxidation is loss of electrons and an increase in oxidation number. Reduction is gain of electrons and a decrease in oxidation number. They happen together.

notes.heading: What are spectator ions?
notes.body: Spectator ions remain chemically unchanged in an aqueous reaction. Remove identical ions on both sides to write the net ionic equation, preserving charge and atom balance.

topics.formula: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss; Reduction Is Gain

practice.question: Balance: Mg + O₂ → MgO.
practice.answer: Use 2 oxygen atoms on the product side, then balance magnesium: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.

practice.question: For Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, identify oxidation and reduction.
practice.answer: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ is oxidation. Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu is reduction. Zinc is the reducing agent because it donates electrons.

practice.question: Balance the equation Al + O₂ → Al₂O₃.
practice.answer: Choose 2Al₂O₃ to make 6 oxygen atoms on the right, requiring 3O₂. This gives 4 aluminium atoms, so the balanced equation is 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃.

practice.question: Write the oxidation half-equation for Mg forming Mg²⁺.
practice.answer: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻. Magnesium loses two electrons, so it is oxidised. Charge is balanced: 0 on the left and +2 − 2 = 0 on the right.

practice.question: For 2Ag⁺ + Cu → 2Ag + Cu²⁺, identify the oxidising agent and explain.
practice.answer: Ag⁺ is the oxidising agent because it accepts electrons and is reduced to Ag. Copper donates electrons and is oxidised to Cu²⁺.

practice.question: For AgNO₃(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq), write the net ionic equation and identify spectator ions.
practice.answer: Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s). Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ remain unchanged in solution and are spectator ions.

topics.tip: Show your reasoning and check the units or restrictions in your final answer.

challenges.question: When balancing a chemical equation, why may coefficients change but subscripts in the substances’ formulae may not?
challenges.answer: Coefficients change the number of particles of an unchanged substance. Subscripts define the substance’s composition; changing them makes a different substance. Balance atom numbers while preserving the identities of reactants and products.

challenges.question: Why must oxidation and reduction occur together in an electron-transfer reaction?
challenges.answer: Electrons lost by one species must be gained by another. The electron donor is oxidised and the electron acceptor is reduced. The total number of electrons transferred balances; free electrons are not created by the overall reaction.

cards.back: Choose 2Al₂O₃ to make 6 oxygen atoms on the right, requiring 3O₂. This gives 4 aluminium atoms, so the balanced equation is 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃.

cards.front: For AgNO₃(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq), write the net ionic equation and identify spectator ions.
cards.back: Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s). Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ remain unchanged in solution and are spectator ions.

cards.front: Balance Fe₂O₃ + CO → Fe + CO₂. Determine the oxidation-number change of iron and carbon, and identify the reducing agent.
cards.back: Balanced equation: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Iron changes from +3 to 0 and is reduced. Carbon changes from +2 in CO to +4 in CO₂ and is oxidised. CO is the reducing agent because it causes iron’s reduction while itself being oxidised.

cards.front: Write balanced half-equations and the overall ionic equation for aluminium reducing Cu²⁺ to copper. Show that electron loss equals electron gain.
cards.back: Oxidation: Al → Al³⁺ + 3e⁻; multiply by 2. Reduction: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu; multiply by 3. Both involve 6 electrons. Overall: 2Al + 3Cu²⁺ → 2Al³⁺ + 3Cu. Atoms and net charge (+6 on each side) are balanced.

cards.front: What happens to oxidation number during oxidation?
cards.back: It increases.

cards.front: Which reactant is the oxidising agent?
cards.back: The species that accepts electrons and is itself reduced.

cards.front: What must balance in an ionic equation besides atoms?
cards.back: Total electric charge.

cards.front: Why should you not change a formula’s subscripts when balancing?
cards.back: That changes the chemical substance instead of only its reacting amount.

topics.subject: physical
topics.title: Energy changes & catalysts

notes.heading: What does enthalpy change mean?
notes.body: ΔH = energy of products − energy of reactants. Negative ΔH indicates an exothermic reaction; positive ΔH indicates endothermic. Label axes on an energy profile.

notes.heading: What is activation energy?
notes.body: Activation energy is the energy barrier from reactants to the transition state. Bond breaking absorbs energy; bond formation releases energy.

notes.heading: How does a catalyst work?
notes.body: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy. It speeds up a reaction without being used up overall and does not change ΔH or the reactant/product energy levels.

practice.question: Reactants have energy 80 kJ and products 30 kJ. Find ΔH and classify the reaction.
practice.answer: ΔH = 30 − 80 = −50 kJ. The reaction is exothermic because products are lower in energy and energy is released.

practice.question: Reactants are at 40 kJ/mol and the peak at 150 kJ/mol. A catalyst lowers the peak to 100. Find both activation energies.
practice.answer: Uncatalysed Eₐ = 150 − 40 = 110 kJ/mol. Catalysed Eₐ = 100 − 40 = 60 kJ/mol. ΔH is unchanged.

practice.question: Products have energy 120 kJ/mol and reactants 75 kJ/mol. Calculate ΔH and classify the reaction.
practice.answer: ΔH = Hproducts − Hreactants = 120 − 75 = +45 kJ/mol. It is endothermic because products have higher energy and energy is absorbed overall.

practice.question: An energy profile has reactants at 50 kJ/mol, products at 20 kJ/mol and the peak at 140 kJ/mol. Find forward and reverse activation energies.
practice.answer: Forward Eₐ = 140 − 50 = 90 kJ/mol. Reverse Eₐ = 140 − 20 = 120 kJ/mol. Forward ΔH is 20 − 50 = −30 kJ/mol.

practice.question: A catalyst lowers the activation energy from 80 to 45 kJ/mol. Does it change ΔH? Explain.
practice.answer: No. The catalyst changes the reaction pathway and lowers the energy barrier, but it does not change the energy levels of the reactants or products. Their difference, ΔH, stays the same.

practice.question: Bond breaking absorbs 500 kJ/mol and bond formation releases 620 kJ/mol for a reaction. Calculate the overall energy change.
practice.answer: ΔH = energy absorbed − energy released = 500 − 620 = −120 kJ/mol. The reaction is exothermic because more energy is released than absorbed.

topics.tip: Show your reasoning and check the units or restrictions in your final answer.

challenges.question: Does adding a catalyst make an endothermic reaction exothermic? Explain using an energy profile.
challenges.answer: No. A catalyst provides a pathway with lower activation energy. It does not change the energies of reactants and products, so their difference, ΔH, and its sign remain unchanged.

challenges.question: A learner says breaking bonds releases the energy that fuels a reaction. Explain what must be compared to decide the overall energy change.
challenges.answer: Breaking bonds requires energy; forming bonds releases energy. Compare the energy absorbed breaking reactant bonds with the energy released forming product bonds. The net difference determines whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.

cards.front: A reaction has reactants at 90 kJ/mol, products at 30 kJ/mol and an uncatalysed peak at 210 kJ/mol. A catalyst lowers the peak to 150. Find ΔH, both forward activation energies and the catalysed reverse activation energy.
cards.back: ΔH = 30 − 90 = −60 kJ/mol, so forward reaction is exothermic. Uncatalysed forward Eₐ = 210 − 90 = 120 kJ/mol. Catalysed forward Eₐ = 150 − 90 = 60 kJ/mol. Catalysed reverse Eₐ = 150 − 30 = 120 kJ/mol. The catalyst does not change ΔH.

cards.front: A proposed explanation says a catalyst speeds up an exothermic reaction by lowering the products’ energy and making ΔH more negative. Correct it using an energy-profile description.

On a profile, draw a lower peak joining the same start and end levels. It changes the rate, not the overall energy released per mole for that reaction.

cards.front: From which level is forward activation energy measured?
cards.back: From reactant energy to the transition-state peak.

cards.front: How is reverse activation energy found on a profile?
cards.back: Peak energy minus product energy.

cards.front: What sign does ΔH have for an exothermic reaction?
cards.back: Negative.

topics.subject: physical
topics.title: Acids, bases & conjugate pairs

notes.heading: What is a Brønsted–Lowry acid?
notes.body: An acid donates a proton (H⁺); a base accepts a proton. This definition describes proton transfer in a reaction, so identify which reactant actually donates or accepts.

notes.heading: How do conjugate pairs differ?
notes.body: An acid and its conjugate base differ by one H⁺. Removing H⁺ lowers the charge by 1; adding H⁺ raises the charge by 1. Water can act as an acid or a base.

notes.heading: What happens when acid meets carbonate?
notes.body: An acid and a carbonate or hydrogen carbonate produce a salt, water and carbon dioxide. CO₂ turns clear limewater milky. Balance the complete reaction.

topics.formula: Acid + base ⇌ conjugate base + conjugate acid

practice.question: In HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻ identify the acid, base and conjugate pairs.
practice.answer: HCl donates H⁺, so is the acid. H₂O accepts it, so is the base. Conjugate pairs are HCl/Cl⁻ and H₂O/H₃O⁺.

practice.question: Balance the reaction between hydrochloric acid and sodium carbonate.
practice.answer: 2HCl + Na₂CO₃ → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. The gas can be identified by turning clear limewater milky.

practice.question: In NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻, identify the acid, base and conjugate pairs.
practice.answer: H₂O donates H⁺ and is the acid; NH₃ accepts H⁺ and is the base. The conjugate pairs are H₂O/OH⁻ and NH₃/NH₄⁺.

practice.question: Give the conjugate base of H₂SO₄ and the conjugate acid of HCO₃⁻.
practice.answer: Removing one H⁺ from H₂SO₄ gives HSO₄⁻. Adding one H⁺ to HCO₃⁻ gives H₂CO₃. A conjugate pair differs by exactly one proton.

practice.question: Balance the reaction between sulfuric acid and sodium hydroxide.
practice.answer: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Two hydroxide ions are required to neutralise the two acidic protons in the complete neutralisation shown.

practice.question: State what amphiprotic means and use water as an example.
practice.answer: An amphiprotic substance can donate or accept H⁺. Water accepts H⁺ to form H₃O⁺ when reacting with an acid, or donates H⁺ to form OH⁻ when reacting with a suitable base.

topics.tip: Show your reasoning and check the units or restrictions in your final answer.

challenges.question: Why is water able to act as an acid in one reaction and a base in another?
challenges.answer: In the Brønsted–Lowry model an acid donates a proton and a base accepts one. Water can donate H⁺ to a stronger base or accept H⁺ from an acid, so its role depends on its reaction partner.

challenges.question: A learner calls HCl and Cl⁻ a conjugate pair, but HCl and OH⁻ another conjugate pair. Which is valid and why?
challenges.answer: HCl and Cl⁻ differ by exactly one proton and form a conjugate acid–base pair. OH⁻ is not HCl after losing one proton; it belongs to the H₂O/OH⁻ pair. Both participating substances in a reaction need not be conjugates of one another.

cards.back: NaHCO₃ + HCl → NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. The gas is carbon dioxide. Bubbling only shows gas formation; passing the gas into clear limewater and observing milkiness supports identifying it as CO₂. Use the prescribed safe laboratory procedure.

topics.subject: physical
topics.title: Moles & stoichiometry

notes.heading: How do you convert mass to moles?
notes.body: Use n = m/M with mass in grams and molar mass in g/mol. A mole contains Avogadro’s number of particles. Say whether the particles are atoms, molecules or formula units.

notes.heading: How do balanced equations give ratios?
notes.body: Equation coefficients give mole ratios, not mass ratios. Convert known mass to moles, use the coefficient ratio, then convert the required moles to mass.

notes.heading: How do you calculate concentration?
notes.body: Molar concentration is moles of solute per dm³ of solution. Convert cm³ to dm³ by dividing by 1 000. For empirical formulae, divide element mole amounts by the smallest.

notes.heading: Balance first, then use the mole ratio
notes.body: Write correct formulae, balance the equation and convert the known quantity into moles. Use coefficients for the mole ratio, then convert the required amount to mass, volume or particle number using the conditions stated. Coefficients are not automatically mass ratios.

topics.formula: n = m/M  •  c = n/V  •  N = nNₐ

practice.question: Find the concentration when 5.85 g NaCl (M = 58.5 g/mol) is dissolved to make 500 cm³ of solution.
For 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, what mass of water forms from 4 g H₂ with excess oxygen? Use M(H₂) = 2 and M(H₂O) = 18 g/mol.
practice.answer: n(H₂) = 4/2 = 2 mol. Ratio H₂:H₂O is 2:2 = 1:1, so 2 mol water forms. m = 2 × 18 = 36 g.

practice.question: Find the number of moles in 22 g of CO₂. Use M(CO₂) = 44 g/mol.
How many molecules are in 0.25 mol of O₂? Use Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
practice.answer: N = nNₐ = 0.25 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.505 × 10²³ molecules. The question asks for molecules, not twice as many oxygen atoms.

practice.question: A solution contains 0.30 mol solute in 750 cm³ of solution. Find its molar concentration.
For 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, calculate the mass of MgO formed from 12 g Mg with excess oxygen. Use M(Mg) = 24 and M(MgO) = 40 g/mol.
practice.answer: n(Mg) = 12/24 = 0.50 mol. The Mg:MgO mole ratio is 1:1, so 0.50 mol MgO forms. Mass = nM = 0.50 × 40 = 20 g.

topics.tip: Show your reasoning and check the units or restrictions in your final answer.

challenges.question: Equal masses of two different substances usually do not contain equal numbers of particles. Explain the missing factor.
challenges.answer: The mole amount is n = m/M. Different substances generally have different molar masses M, so equal masses give different mole amounts and particle numbers. Equal moles, not equal masses, contain equal numbers of the specified particles.

challenges.question: A balanced equation uses a 1:2 ratio of reactants. Why is this not automatically a 1:2 mass ratio?
challenges.answer: The coefficients give particle-number or mole ratios. Mass also depends on each substance’s molar mass. Convert the stoichiometric mole amounts into masses using m = nM before comparing masses.

cards.front: How do you convert mass to moles?
cards.back: Use n = m/M with mass in grams and molar mass in g/mol. A mole contains Avogadro’s number of particles. Say whether the particles are atoms, molecules or formula units.

cards.front: How do balanced equations give ratios?
cards.back: Equation coefficients give mole ratios, not mass ratios. Convert known mass to moles, use the coefficient ratio, then convert the required moles to mass.

cards.front: How do you calculate concentration?
cards.back: Molar concentration is moles of solute per dm³ of solution. Convert cm³ to dm³ by dividing by 1 000. For empirical formulae, divide element mole amounts by the smallest.

cards.front: Find the concentration when 5.85 g NaCl (M = 58.5 g/mol) is dissolved to make 500 cm³ of solution.
For 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, what mass of water forms from 4 g H₂ with excess oxygen? Use M(H₂) = 2 and M(H₂O) = 18 g/mol.
cards.back: n(H₂) = 4/2 = 2 mol. Ratio H₂:H₂O is 2:2 = 1:1, so 2 mol water forms. m = 2 × 18 = 36 g.

cards.front: Find the number of moles in 22 g of CO₂. Use M(CO₂) = 44 g/mol.

cards.back: N = nNₐ = 0.25 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.505 × 10²³ molecules. The question asks for molecules, not twice as many oxygen atoms.

cards.front: A solution contains 0.30 mol solute in 750 cm³ of solution. Find its molar concentration.
For 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, calculate the mass of MgO formed from 12 g Mg with excess oxygen. Use M(Mg) = 24 and M(MgO) = 40 g/mol.
cards.back: n(Mg) = 12/24 = 0.50 mol. The Mg:MgO mole ratio is 1:1, so 0.50 mol MgO forms. Mass = nM = 0.50 × 40 = 20 g.

cards.front: For 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, mix 6 g H₂ with 32 g O₂. Use molar masses 2, 32 and 18 g/mol respectively. Identify the limiting reagent, the mass of water formed and the mass of excess reactant left.
cards.back: H₂ = 6/2 = 3 mol and O₂ = 32/32 = 1 mol. One mole O₂ needs 2 mol H₂, so O₂ is limiting. It makes 2 mol H₂O = 2 × 18 = 36 g. H₂ remaining = 1 mol = 2 g. Check mass: initial 38 g = 36 g water + 2 g hydrogen.

cards.front: A 12.5 g sample of CuSO₄·nH₂O is heated to constant mass, leaving 8.0 g anhydrous CuSO₄. Use M(CuSO₄) = 160 g/mol and M(H₂O) = 18 g/mol. Find n and explain the mole-ratio step.
cards.back: Water lost = 12.5 − 8.0 = 4.5 g, so n(H₂O) = 4.5/18 = 0.25 mol. Anhydrous CuSO₄ = 8.0/160 = 0.05 mol. Divide both by 0.05: CuSO₄:H₂O = 1:5. Therefore n = 5. This assumes the mass loss is water and heating leaves the stated anhydrous solid.

cards.front: What do balanced-equation coefficients compare?
cards.back: Numbers of reacting particles or moles, not direct mass ratios.

cards.front: How do you identify a limiting reagent?
cards.back: Compare available moles with the stoichiometric amounts required, then find which is exhausted first.

cards.front: What is removed when a hydrate is heated to the specified anhydrous form?
cards.back: Water of crystallisation, under the assumptions of the experiment.

cards.front: Why convert cm³ to dm³ for c = n/V in mol/dm³?
cards.back: Volume units must match the units required for concentration; divide cm³ by 1 000.

cards.front: Equal masses of two different substances usually do not contain equal numbers of particles. Explain the missing factor.
cards.back: The mole amount is n = m/M. Different substances generally have different molar masses M, so equal masses give different mole amounts and particle numbers. Equal moles, not equal masses, contain equal numbers of the specified particles.

cards.back: The coefficients give particle-number or mole ratios. Mass also depends on each substance’s molar mass. Convert the stoichiometric mole amounts into masses using m = nM before comparing masses.

cards.front: Balance first, then use the mole ratio
cards.back: Write correct formulae, balance the equation and convert the known quantity into moles. Use coefficients for the mole ratio, then convert the required amount to mass, volume or particle number using the conditions stated. Coefficients are not automatically mass ratios.

topics.subject: life
topics.title: Cells & membrane transport

notes.heading: What do the main organelles do?
notes.body: The nucleus contains genetic information; mitochondria carry out most aerobic ATP production; chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis. Plant cells also have a cellulose cell wall and usually a large permanent vacuole.

notes.heading: How do diffusion and osmosis differ?
notes.body: Diffusion is the net movement of particles down a concentration gradient. Osmosis is the net movement of water through a selectively permeable membrane from higher to lower water potential.

notes.heading: When does transport require energy?
notes.body: Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient using energy and transport proteins. Facilitated diffusion uses membrane proteins but moves down a gradient without direct ATP input.

practice.question: A plant cell is placed in pure water. Explain why it becomes turgid.
practice.answer: Water enters by osmosis because the outside has higher water potential. The vacuole expands and pushes the cytoplasm against the cell wall. The strong wall resists further expansion, creating turgor.

practice.question: Why does active transport require ATP while facilitated diffusion does not?
practice.answer: Active transport moves particles against their concentration gradient and needs an energy supply. Facilitated diffusion moves down the gradient through proteins, so no direct ATP input is needed.

practice.question: Give two structures usually present in a plant cell but absent from an animal cell, and state one function of each.
practice.answer: A cellulose cell wall provides support and helps prevent excessive expansion. Chloroplasts in photosynthetic plant cells absorb light and carry out photosynthesis. Not every plant cell contains chloroplasts.

practice.question: A red blood cell is placed in a solution with a lower water potential than its cytoplasm. Predict and explain its change in size.
practice.answer: Water leaves the cell by osmosis through the selectively permeable membrane, moving toward the lower water potential. The cell loses volume and shrinks.

practice.question: A cell accumulates a mineral ion even though the ion concentration is already greater inside than outside. Identify the transport process and explain its energy requirement.
practice.answer: This is active transport because movement is against the concentration gradient. Transport proteins use an energy supply, often from ATP, to move the ions in that direction.

practice.question: Explain how facilitated diffusion differs from simple diffusion.
practice.answer: Both involve net movement down a concentration gradient without direct ATP input. Facilitated diffusion uses membrane proteins, whereas simple diffusion crosses the lipid bilayer without a transport protein.

topics.tip: Show your reasoning and check the units or restrictions in your final answer.

challenges.question: A plant cell is placed in dilute water. Explain why it becomes turgid rather than continuing to swell like an unprotected membrane bag.
challenges.answer: Water enters by osmosis across the selectively permeable membrane. The rigid cell wall resists expansion, and pressure builds against it. The pressure counteracts further net water uptake; the membrane alone does not provide that rigid support.

challenges.question: Why does the fact that a cell is alive not mean every substance must be moved across its membrane by active transport?
challenges.answer: Diffusion and osmosis are passive processes driven by gradients and occur in living cells without direct energy input for each movement. Active transport uses cellular energy to move substances against an electrochemical gradient or through energy-coupled mechanisms.

cards.back: Both involve net movement down a concentration gradient without direct ATP input. Facilitated diffusion uses membrane proteins, whereas simple diffusion crosses the lipid bilayer without a transport protein.

cards.front: Equal potato cylinders are placed in solutions A, B and C. Their masses change by +12%, 0% and −8%. Infer the relative water potentials of the solutions and potato tissue. Explain why the result in B does not mean water molecules stopped moving.
cards.back: A has higher water potential than the tissue, so net water entry increases mass. C has lower water potential, so net water loss decreases mass. B is approximately in balance with the tissue under these conditions. In B, water still moves both ways across membranes, but there is no net transfer detectable by this mass measurement.

cards.front: A cell takes up ion X against its concentration gradient. A treatment that reduces ATP production sharply reduces X uptake but does not stop the passage of small non-polar molecules through the membrane. Explain the two transport patterns and identify a limitation of the evidence.
cards.back: X uptake is consistent with energy-dependent active transport through proteins. Small non-polar molecules can cross the lipid bilayer by simple diffusion down their gradient without direct ATP use. The result supports this interpretation but does not prove one specific transporter mechanism; the treatment may have other effects on cell health or membranes. A suitable viability control is needed.

cards.front: What does zero net osmosis mean?
cards.back: Movement in both directions is balanced; individual water molecules still move.

cards.front: Which plant-cell structure resists swelling as turgor increases?
cards.back: The cell wall.

cards.front: What does selectively permeable mean?
cards.back: Some substances cross more readily than others; permeability depends on membrane and particle properties.

cards.front: How do you calculate percentage mass change?
cards.back: (Final mass − initial mass)/initial mass × 100%.

topics.subject: life
topics.title: Mitosis & the cell cycle

notes.heading: What happens before mitosis?
notes.body: During interphase the cell grows and, in S phase, replicates DNA. Each duplicated chromosome has two sister chromatids before division. DNA replication is essential for equal genetic information.

notes.heading: What is the PMAT sequence?
notes.body: Prophase: chromosomes condense. Metaphase: chromosomes line up at the equator. Anaphase: sister chromatids separate to opposite poles. Telophase: nuclei reform; cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm.

notes.heading: What is the outcome of mitosis?
notes.body: In normal mitosis, two daughter cells keep the parent cell’s chromosome number and are genetically identical, apart from possible mutations. Mitosis supports growth, repair and asexual reproduction.

notes.heading: DNA copying and cell division are separate stages
notes.body: DNA replication precedes mitosis. Mitosis distributes copies into daughter nuclei and cytokinesis divides the cell. Keep the distinction between a chromosome, its sister chromatids and the amount of DNA clear when explaining why chromosome number is normally maintained.

practice.question: A body cell with 6 chromosomes divides by normal mitosis. How many daughter cells form and how many chromosomes are in each?
practice.answer: Two daughter cells form. Each has 6 chromosomes, the same chromosome number as the parent cell.

practice.question: Distinguish metaphase from anaphase.
practice.answer: At metaphase, duplicated chromosomes align at the equator. At anaphase, sister chromatids separate at the centromeres and move to opposite poles.

practice.question: A cell is observed with condensed chromosomes arranged at the equator. Identify the mitotic phase and the next main event.
practice.answer: This is metaphase. In the next phase, anaphase, sister chromatids separate at their centromeres and move toward opposite poles.

practice.question: Why must DNA replicate before normal mitosis?
practice.answer: Replication creates two copies of each chromosome’s genetic information. When sister chromatids separate, each daughter nucleus can receive a complete, equivalent set.

practice.question: A body cell with 8 chromosomes undergoes two successive rounds of normal mitosis. How many cells result, and how many chromosomes are in each?
practice.answer: The first division makes 2 cells; each divides again to make 4 cells in total. Each daughter cell retains 8 chromosomes, assuming normal division and no chromosome loss.

practice.question: Distinguish mitosis from cytokinesis.
practice.answer: Mitosis divides replicated nuclear genetic material into daughter nuclei. Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm and separates the cell into two daughter cells; the processes are connected but distinct.

topics.tip: Do not confuse DNA replication in interphase with chromosome separation in anaphase. The supplied 2022 memo has an inconsistent stage description.

challenges.question: A cell copies its DNA before mitosis. Why does this not mean each daughter cell must end with twice the original chromosome number?
challenges.answer: DNA replication produces sister chromatids for each chromosome. During mitosis these separate into two nuclei, giving each daughter a copy of the original chromosome set. DNA replication and chromosome counting must be distinguished.

challenges.question: Why would separating sister chromatids before they are properly attached to the spindle threaten genetic continuity?
challenges.answer: Accurate spindle attachment helps distribute one copy of each chromosome to each daughter nucleus. Premature or incorrect separation can produce unequal chromosome sets. The checkpoint protects the distribution process rather than simply making division faster.

cards.front: A normal diploid cell has 4 chromosomes before DNA replication. State its chromosome and chromatid counts at metaphase, then the chromosome count in each daughter cell after normal mitosis. Explain the counting convention.
cards.back: After replication, metaphase still has 4 chromosomes, each with two sister chromatids, so there are 8 chromatids. Chromosome number is counted by centromeres, not by DNA copies. When division is completed normally, each daughter cell has 4 chromosomes. Replication doubles DNA content without doubling metaphase chromosome number.

cards.front: In a cell with 6 duplicated chromosomes, one pair of sister chromatids fails to separate while the others segregate normally. Predict the daughter-cell chromosome numbers and explain why normal mitosis is important for tissue repair.
cards.back: The affected chromosome’s two chromatids go to one daughter instead of one to each. With all other segregation normal, the daughters receive 7 and 5 chromosomes rather than 6 each. Normal mitosis preserves the full chromosome complement during growth and repair; unequal segregation can disrupt cell function. The numbers assume the single stated segregation error.

cards.front: At which stage are sister chromatids normally separated?
cards.back: Anaphase.

cards.front: Does DNA replication occur during mitosis?
cards.back: It occurs before mitosis, in the S phase of interphase.

cards.front: What distinguishes a chromosome count from a chromatid count at metaphase?
cards.back: A duplicated chromosome has one joined centromere region but two sister chromatids.

cards.front: What is cytokinesis?
cards.back: Division of the cytoplasm to form separate daughter cells.

topics.subject: life
topics.title: Enzymes & biological molecules

notes.heading: How does an enzyme act?
notes.body: An enzyme is a biological catalyst. Its active site binds a suitable substrate, helping a reaction proceed with a lower activation energy. Products leave and the enzyme can be reused.

notes.heading: Why do temperature and pH matter?
notes.body: Activity usually increases with temperature up to an optimum. Excess heat or unsuitable pH can alter the active-site shape. Denaturation reduces binding and activity; cooling is not the same as denaturing.

notes.heading: What happens as substrate increases?
notes.body: At fixed enzyme concentration the reaction rate rises, then levels off as active sites become saturated. More substrate cannot increase the maximum rate unless more active enzyme is available.

practice.question: Why can a high temperature reduce the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction?
practice.answer: Heat can disrupt bonds maintaining enzyme shape. The active site changes, so fewer substrates bind and fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form.

practice.question: An enzyme reaction stops getting faster when more substrate is added. Explain.
practice.answer: The available active sites are occupied: the enzymes are saturated. Enzyme concentration is now limiting, so adding substrate alone does not raise the maximum rate.

practice.question: Explain why lactase acts on lactose but not on every other food molecule.
practice.answer: The shape and chemical properties of lactase’s active site allow suitable interaction with lactose. Other molecules may not bind correctly, so enzyme specificity limits which reactions it catalyses.

practice.question: An enzyme reaction runs slowly at 5°C but speeds up after warming to its optimum. Does the initial slow rate prove denaturation?
practice.answer: No. Low temperature usually reduces particle movement and successful encounters, slowing the reaction. Recovery after warming is consistent with the enzyme retaining its functional shape.

practice.question: An enzyme concentration is doubled while substrate remains plentiful and other conditions stay optimal. Predict the initial effect on reaction rate.
practice.answer: More enzyme supplies more available active sites, so more substrate can be processed at once and the initial rate should increase. The exact increase depends on the experimental conditions.

practice.question: Name a test for starch and state a positive result.
practice.answer: Add iodine solution to the sample under appropriate laboratory instructions. A blue-black colour indicates starch; iodine solution remaining yellow-brown is a negative result.

topics.tip: Show your reasoning and check the units or restrictions in your final answer.

challenges.question: An enzyme reaction becomes slower above its optimum temperature. Why does “the particles are moving more slowly” fail as an explanation?
challenges.answer: Higher temperature generally increases molecular motion. Above the optimum, disruption of the enzyme’s structure can change its active site, reducing successful substrate binding and catalysis. Slower reaction rate can therefore result despite faster particle motion.

challenges.question: Why does doubling substrate concentration eventually stop doubling reaction rate when enzyme concentration is fixed?
challenges.answer: At high substrate concentration, enzyme active sites are occupied much of the time. The rate becomes limited by the enzyme’s available sites and turnover. Adding more substrate then has little effect unless more active enzyme becomes available.

cards.back: At high substrate concentration, nearly all available active sites are occupied, so enzyme concentration limits the rate. More substrate alone gives little increase. Adding active enzyme provides additional active sites and should increase the maximum attainable rate if other conditions and substrate supply remain suitable. The data do not show that the enzyme was consumed.

cards.front: Two enzyme samples are treated differently: A is cooled to 5°C and B heated to 90°C. Both are later returned to the same optimum temperature and tested identically. A recovers its activity but B does not. Explain and propose one controlled variable needed for the comparison.
cards.back: Cooling can slow molecular movement without permanently disrupting the enzyme, so A can recover after warming. High heat can denature B, altering the active site so normal binding does not return. Keep pH, enzyme amount, substrate concentration and testing time equivalent. A comparison should also check that both samples underwent the same final assay conditions.

cards.front: Are enzymes used up overall during the reactions they catalyse?
cards.back: No. They can be reused, although they can be damaged or denatured.

cards.front: What does an enzyme-rate plateau at high substrate often suggest?
cards.back: Available enzyme active sites have become limiting.

cards.front: What is activation energy?
cards.back: The energy barrier that reacting particles must overcome for a reaction pathway.

cards.front: Why does a negative starch test not by itself prove an enzyme worked?
cards.back: Starch may have been absent initially or another factor may explain the result; compare appropriate controls.

topics.subject: life
topics.title: Digestion & blood-glucose control

notes.heading: What are digestion and absorption?
notes.body: Digestion breaks large food molecules into smaller soluble molecules. Absorption moves these molecules across the intestinal wall into blood or lymph. Most nutrient absorption occurs in the small intestine.

notes.heading: What does bile do?
notes.body: The liver produces bile; the gall bladder stores and concentrates it. Bile emulsifies fats into droplets, increasing surface area for lipase. Emulsification is physical and bile is not a digestive enzyme.

notes.heading: How is blood glucose regulated?
notes.body: High glucose stimulates pancreatic insulin release, increasing glucose uptake and glycogen formation. Low glucose stimulates glucagon, promoting liver glycogen breakdown and glucose release. This is negative feedback.

topics.formula: High glucose → insulin  •  Low glucose → glucagon

practice.question: Explain how villi improve absorption.
practice.answer: Villi and microvilli increase surface area. A thin epithelium shortens diffusion distance. Blood capillaries and lacteals carry absorbed nutrients away, helping maintain transport gradients.

practice.question: Describe the response to a rise in blood glucose after a meal.
practice.answer: Pancreatic beta cells release insulin. Body cells increase glucose uptake and the liver and muscles store glucose as glycogen. Blood glucose falls toward its regulated range.

practice.question: Distinguish mechanical digestion from chemical digestion and give one example of each.
practice.answer: Mechanical digestion physically breaks food into smaller pieces, such as chewing. Chemical digestion breaks chemical bonds in large molecules, for example amylase acting on starch.

practice.question: Explain why emulsifying fats increases the effectiveness of lipase.
practice.answer: Emulsification breaks large fat globules into smaller droplets, increasing total surface area. More fat surface is available for lipase action. Bile itself is not the fat-digesting enzyme.

practice.question: Blood glucose falls between meals. Name the main pancreatic hormone involved in raising it and describe its effect on the liver.
practice.answer: Glucagon is released. It promotes breakdown of liver glycogen and release of glucose into the blood, helping return blood glucose toward its regulated range.

practice.question: Why does the small intestine have both a large surface area and a good blood supply?
practice.answer: Villi and microvilli provide a large area for absorption. Blood carries many absorbed nutrients away and helps maintain concentration gradients, supporting continued uptake.

topics.tip: Show your reasoning and check the units or restrictions in your final answer.

challenges.question: Why is digesting starch not the same thing as absorbing glucose?
challenges.answer: Digestion breaks large starch molecules into smaller soluble molecules, ultimately including glucose. Absorption transfers these small molecules across the intestinal epithelium into transport systems. Chemical breakdown and movement across a barrier are different processes.

challenges.question: Blood glucose rises after a meal. Explain why insulin’s response is called negative feedback, even though insulin secretion increases.
challenges.answer: The response opposes the original change: insulin promotes processes that lower elevated blood glucose toward the regulated range. “Negative” describes opposition to the disturbance, not a decrease in every variable in the pathway.

cards.back: Digestion breaks large food molecules into smaller soluble molecules. Absorption moves these molecules across the intestinal wall into blood or lymph. Most nutrient absorption occurs in the small intestine.

cards.front: What does bile do?
cards.back: The liver produces bile; the gall bladder stores and concentrates it. Bile emulsifies fats into droplets, increasing surface area for lipase. Emulsification is physical and bile is not a digestive enzyme.

cards.front: How is blood glucose regulated?
cards.back: High glucose stimulates pancreatic insulin release, increasing glucose uptake and glycogen formation. Low glucose stimulates glucagon, promoting liver glycogen breakdown and glucose release. This is negative feedback.

cards.front: Explain how villi improve absorption.
cards.back: Villi and microvilli increase surface area. A thin epithelium shortens diffusion distance. Blood capillaries and lacteals carry absorbed nutrients away, helping maintain transport gradients.

cards.front: Describe the response to a rise in blood glucose after a meal.
cards.back: Pancreatic beta cells release insulin. Body cells increase glucose uptake and the liver and muscles store glucose as glycogen. Blood glucose falls toward its regulated range.

cards.front: Distinguish mechanical digestion from chemical digestion and give one example of each.
cards.back: Mechanical digestion physically breaks food into smaller pieces, such as chewing. Chemical digestion breaks chemical bonds in large molecules, for example amylase acting on starch.

cards.front: Explain why emulsifying fats increases the effectiveness of lipase.
cards.back: Emulsification breaks large fat globules into smaller droplets, increasing total surface area. More fat surface is available for lipase action. Bile itself is not the fat-digesting enzyme.

cards.front: Blood glucose falls between meals. Name the main pancreatic hormone involved in raising it and describe its effect on the liver.
cards.back: Glucagon is released. It promotes breakdown of liver glycogen and release of glucose into the blood, helping return blood glucose toward its regulated range.

cards.front: Why does the small intestine have both a large surface area and a good blood supply?
cards.back: Villi and microvilli provide a large area for absorption. Blood carries many absorbed nutrients away and helps maintain concentration gradients, supporting continued uptake.

cards.front: A diagram claims bile chemically digests fats and the small intestine mainly stores the absorbed glucose. Correct both statements and trace how absorbed glucose can be stored after a meal.
cards.back: Bile emulsifies fat physically, producing small droplets that provide more surface for lipase; it is not the enzyme chemically hydrolysing fat. The small intestine is a major site of nutrient absorption. Absorbed glucose enters blood and can be taken up by tissues; insulin promotes storage as glycogen in the liver and muscles when glucose is high.

cards.front: A meal raises blood glucose, followed later by a return toward its regulated range. Describe the negative-feedback response. Then explain why the graph alone cannot establish that the person has normal insulin sensitivity.
cards.back: The rise stimulates pancreatic insulin release. Insulin supports glucose uptake and glycogen formation, tending to lower blood glucose and reduce the original stimulus. A glucose graph alone does not measure insulin levels, sensitivity or other influences such as meal size, exercise and timing. Multiple mechanisms can produce similar curves, so a clinical conclusion would require more evidence.

cards.front: Where is bile produced and where is it stored?
cards.back: Produced by the liver; stored and concentrated in the gall bladder.

cards.front: Which hormone mainly promotes release of glucose from liver glycogen when blood glucose is low?
cards.back: Glucagon.

cards.front: Why is blood-glucose control negative feedback?
cards.back: The response counteracts the initial rise or fall rather than amplifying it.

cards.front: What is the distinction between digestion and absorption?
cards.back: Digestion breaks food molecules down; absorption transfers suitable products across the gut wall.

cards.front: Why is digesting starch not the same thing as absorbing glucose?
cards.back: Digestion breaks large starch molecules into smaller soluble molecules, ultimately including glucose. Absorption transfers these small molecules across the intestinal epithelium into transport systems. Chemical breakdown and movement across a barrier are different processes.

cards.front: Blood glucose rises after a meal. Explain why insulin’s response is called negative feedback, even though insulin secretion increases.
cards.back: The response opposes the original change: insulin promotes processes that lower elevated blood glucose toward the regulated range. “Negative” describes opposition to the disturbance, not a decrease in every variable in the pathway.

topics.subject: life
topics.title: Photosynthesis & cellular respiration

notes.heading: What does photosynthesis achieve?
notes.body: In chloroplasts, light energy supports the conversion of carbon dioxide and water into organic molecules, with oxygen released. Chlorophyll absorbs light. Plants build biomass from the products.

notes.heading: What does respiration achieve?
notes.body: Cellular respiration transfers energy from organic molecules to ATP. Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm; most aerobic ATP production involves mitochondria. Plants respire as well as photosynthesise.

notes.heading: How are the processes connected?
notes.body: Photosynthesis stores energy in organic molecules; respiration makes that energy available for cell work. Matter cycles between organisms and the environment, but energy flows and is eventually dissipated as heat.

notes.heading: Separate the processes and their roles
notes.body: Photosynthesis stores energy in organic molecules using light; cellular respiration makes energy available for cellular processes. Living plant cells respire as well as photosynthesise. Explain an investigation’s result in terms of the relevant process, controlled variables and a suitable comparison.

practice.question: Name the reactants and products in the simplified photosynthesis equation.
practice.answer: Reactants are carbon dioxide and water, using light energy. Products are glucose and oxygen.

practice.question: Do plants respire at night? Explain.
practice.answer: Yes. Living plant cells require ATP continuously, so respiration continues day and night. Photosynthesis depends on light and does not proceed normally in darkness.

practice.question: Explain why a plant may show no net carbon-dioxide exchange at a particular light intensity.
practice.answer: At the compensation point, carbon dioxide uptake by photosynthesis equals carbon dioxide release by respiration. Both processes continue, but their opposing rates balance, giving no net exchange.

practice.question: Name the pigment that absorbs light for photosynthesis and the organelle containing it.
practice.answer: The pigment is chlorophyll, located in the thylakoid membranes within chloroplasts.

practice.question: State the reactants and main products of aerobic cellular respiration in a simplified equation.
practice.answer: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water, with energy transferred to ATP and released as heat. A balanced summary is C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O.

practice.question: A green plant is kept in darkness. Which continues: respiration, photosynthesis, both or neither? Explain.
practice.answer: Respiration continues in living cells to supply ATP. Photosynthesis cannot proceed normally without light energy, so the two processes do not both continue normally in darkness.

topics.tip: Show your reasoning and check the units or restrictions in your final answer.

challenges.question: A green plant is kept in the dark overnight. Does it stop cellular respiration? Explain why photosynthesis and respiration have different light requirements.
challenges.answer: Respiration continues in living plant cells to release usable energy from organic molecules. Photosynthesis requires light for its light-dependent reactions and cannot sustain net photosynthesis in darkness. Plants both photosynthesise and respire; respiration is not restricted to animals.

challenges.question: Why does a higher light intensity fail to increase photosynthesis indefinitely?
challenges.answer: Another factor can become limiting, such as carbon dioxide availability, temperature or the capacity of the photosynthetic machinery. A process controlled by several factors will not increase indefinitely when only one is changed.

cards.front: A plant releases 3 units of CO₂ per hour in darkness. At moderate light it takes up a net 5 units per hour. Assuming respiration remains 3 units per hour, calculate gross CO₂ uptake by photosynthesis and explain a limitation of that assumption.
cards.back: Net uptake = gross photosynthetic uptake − respiratory release. Thus 5 = gross − 3, so gross uptake = 8 units/hour. This calculation assumes the respiratory rate is unchanged between darkness and light; real rates can vary with temperature, physiology and other conditions.

cards.front: An illuminated plant is given labelled carbon dioxide and later the label appears in its sugars. Explain the inference, then describe how some labelled carbon might return to the air and why energy is not recycled in the same way.

cards.back: In the cytoplasm.

cards.front: Do plant cells use ATP?
cards.back: Yes. Plants respire and use ATP for cellular work as animals do.

cards.front: What is the main purpose of chlorophyll in photosynthesis?
cards.back: To absorb light energy.

topics.subject: life
topics.title: Plant transport & adaptations

notes.heading: What do xylem and phloem transport?
notes.body: Xylem carries water and mineral ions mainly from roots toward leaves through mostly dead conducting cells. Phloem translocates dissolved organic substances between sources and sinks through living tissue.

notes.heading: How do stomata open?
notes.body: Guard cells take up solutes, lowering their water potential. Water enters by osmosis and guard cells become turgid, opening the pore. Water loss makes them flaccid and closes it.

notes.heading: How do leaves limit water loss?
notes.body: A thick waxy cuticle, reduced leaf area, hairs or sunken stomata can reduce water loss. Explain how a named feature works in the environment; a feature is not useful in every habitat.

topics.formula: Water enters guard cells → turgor increases → pore opens

practice.question: Give two differences between xylem and phloem.
practice.answer: Xylem transports water/mineral ions and its main conducting cells are dead at maturity. Phloem transports sugars/other organic solutes and its conducting tissue is living.

practice.question: Explain why a waxy cuticle benefits a plant in a dry habitat.
practice.answer: The waxy layer limits evaporation from the leaf surface. This reduces water loss when water is scarce and helps the plant maintain cell turgor.

practice.question: Explain how root hairs help a plant absorb water and mineral ions.
practice.answer: Root hairs greatly increase the surface area in contact with soil water. Water can enter by osmosis when water potential favours entry, while ions cross membranes by appropriate transport processes, including active transport.

practice.question: Guard cells lose water. Predict the effect on the stomatal pore and water loss.
practice.answer: The guard cells become less turgid and the pore tends to close. This reduces transpiration through the stomata, although it also limits gas exchange.

practice.question: Give two leaf features that can reduce water loss in a dry habitat and explain each.
practice.answer: A thick waxy cuticle limits evaporation from the surface. Reduced leaf area decreases the surface exposed for water loss. Other justified features include hairs or sunken stomata that maintain a humid boundary layer.

practice.question: Why can phloem transport be described in terms of sources and sinks rather than simply upward movement?
practice.answer: A source supplies organic solutes, for example a photosynthesising leaf. A sink uses or stores them, for example a growing root or fruit. Sources and sinks occur in different positions, so transport is not described by one fixed upward direction.

topics.tip: Show your reasoning and check the units or restrictions in your final answer.

challenges.question: Closing stomata helps conserve water. Why can this also reduce a plant’s photosynthetic rate?
challenges.answer: Stomatal closure reduces water-vapour loss but also restricts carbon dioxide entering the leaf. Lower internal CO₂ can limit carbon fixation. The plant faces a trade-off between water conservation and gas exchange.

challenges.question: Why can a thin leaf be helpful for diffusion while a thick waxy cuticle is helpful in a dry habitat? Explain the different demands.
challenges.answer: A thin leaf shortens diffusion distances for gases. A waxy cuticle reduces uncontrolled water loss. Adaptations balance resource exchange and conservation rather than maximising only one feature; stomata regulate much of the gas exchange.

cards.front: What main materials does xylem transport?
cards.back: Water and dissolved mineral ions.

cards.front: What does phloem translocation move between sources and sinks?
cards.back: Dissolved organic substances such as sugars.

cards.front: Why can moving air increase transpiration?
cards.back: It can remove the humid boundary layer around a leaf.

cards.front: What happens to guard-cell turgor when water leaves them?
