topics.subject: english
topics.title: Transactional writing: purpose & register

notes.heading: Plan for a real audience
notes.body: Identify the writer’s role, recipient, purpose, format and required content before drafting. A diary entry can explore a private immediate response; a letter of application presents a relevant case to an organisation. Choose details and register to fit that relationship rather than using the same voice for every form.

notes.heading: Make structure serve the purpose
notes.body: The July scope lists a friendly letter, letter of application, magazine article, diary entry and speech. Revise the conventions in the teacher’s handbook or examples, including appropriate openings and closings. Organise paragraphs so each advances the task; do not let a memorised template displace the actual content requested.

notes.heading: Draft, then edit for effect
notes.body: Plan a few distinct ideas and develop them coherently. Check whether the opening establishes purpose, the middle provides relevant detail and the ending achieves a suitable final impression. Edit agreement, punctuation, tense, repetition and word count. Formal writing can be clear and direct; complicated wording is not a requirement for quality.

practice.question: What changes when the same event is described in a diary and in a formal complaint?
practice.answer: Audience and purpose change. A diary may explore private feelings, while a complaint should identify the problem, provide relevant facts and request a reasonable response in an appropriate register.

practice.question: Write a concise original opening for an application to join a school reading committee.
practice.answer: “I would like to apply to join the school reading committee. My experience organising our class book exchange would help me contribute to its reading events.” The opening states purpose and a relevant reason.

practice.question: Why should a magazine article’s heading relate closely to its content?
practice.answer: It sets expectations and invites the intended audience to read. A striking heading that promises a different subject may undermine coherence and credibility.

practice.question: What is the risk of using slang in a letter of application?
practice.answer: It may be inappropriate for the relationship with the recipient and weaken the impression of professionalism. The issue is suitability for audience and purpose, not that informal language is always wrong.

practice.question: How can a speech conclusion connect to its introduction?
practice.answer: It can return to an opening image, question or idea and show how the speech’s argument has developed it. The link should reinforce the final message rather than repeat the whole speech.

practice.question: Why is a correctly formatted letter not automatically a successful response?
practice.answer: The content may fail to answer the task, suit the audience or develop a clear purpose. Format is one part of an effective response, alongside relevant ideas, organisation and language.

challenges.question: Can two different registers both be appropriate for the same writing form? Explain with a letter.
challenges.answer: Yes. A friendly letter to a close relative and a letter to an unfamiliar organisation use the same broad medium but different relationships and purposes. Format alone does not determine every language choice.

challenges.question: An application lists many achievements but never relates them to the role. Why might a shorter application be more persuasive?
challenges.answer: Relevant evidence matters more than the number of claims. A shorter response that explains how selected experience meets the role’s needs creates a clearer case for the recipient.

cards.front: What five things should you identify before writing?
cards.back: Role, audience, purpose, format and required content.

cards.front: What is register?
cards.back: Language choices suited to the situation, relationship and level of formality.

cards.front: What is coherence?
cards.back: The logical connection of ideas into a meaningful whole.

topics.subject: english
topics.title: Prepared speaking, reading & recital

notes.heading: Write for listening
notes.body: A prepared speech needs a clear introduction, a well-organised body and a purposeful conclusion. Make transitions audible, explain unfamiliar ideas and use relevant evidence. The workbook recommends preparation and research; a dramatic performance is not a substitute for a coherent formal speech.

notes.heading: Make delivery support meaning
notes.body: Practise pronunciation, pace, volume, pauses, eye contact and natural gesture. In prepared reading, phrasing should clarify sentence structure and tone. In poetry recital, stress and pauses should reveal the poem’s meaning rather than impose an identical sing-song rhythm on every line.

notes.heading: Use the actual rubric
notes.body: Compare a rehearsal with the posted reading or recital rubric. Distinguish content preparation from delivery, and select one improvement for the next rehearsal. Know the piece well enough to communicate with the audience; expressive delivery should serve meaning, not distract from it.

practice.question: Why can speaking more slowly at an important point help an audience?
practice.answer: It gives listeners time to process a key idea and can signal emphasis. Vary pace deliberately; making the entire speech unnaturally slow may weaken its flow.

practice.question: How can a speaker establish purpose without simply announcing “My speech is about…”?
practice.answer: Open with a relevant question, brief example or striking idea, then connect it clearly to the topic and direction of the speech. The device should serve the purpose rather than be an unrelated performance.

practice.question: Why should a reader pause at a change in meaning rather than at every printed line ending?
practice.answer: Sentence structure and punctuation may continue across a line break. Phrasing should make the meaning clear; an automatic pause at each line can distort a sentence or poem.

practice.question: What is one useful way to rehearse with a rubric?
practice.answer: Choose a criterion such as audibility or organisation, practise the whole section, obtain specific feedback against that criterion, and rehearse again with one planned change.

practice.question: Why can looking up from notes improve a prepared speech?
practice.answer: It helps maintain audience contact and allows the speaker to notice whether listeners are following. Preparation should make these moments possible without losing the thread of the argument.

practice.question: Explain why louder delivery is not always more expressive delivery.
practice.answer: Expression also depends on pace, stress, tone and pause. A consistently loud voice can flatten differences in meaning; use volume suitable for the audience and room.

challenges.question: A recital is fluent but its dramatic emphasis contradicts the words. Has fluent memorisation alone met the purpose? Explain.
challenges.answer: No. Fluency supports communication, but the delivery must demonstrate understanding of the text. Stress and pauses should be justified by the poem’s voice, situation and movement of ideas.

challenges.question: Two speakers use identical words. Why might one be easier to understand?
challenges.answer: Phrasing, pace, articulation, emphasis and audience contact influence how listeners process the message. Delivery can clarify relationships between ideas even when the written text is the same.

cards.back: Grouping words and using pauses to make grammar and meaning clear.

cards.front: What should gesture support?
cards.back: The meaning and purpose of the speech rather than unrelated movement.

cards.front: What makes rehearsal feedback useful?
cards.back: It identifies a specific observable feature and a practical change.

cards.front: Why learn a poem’s meaning before reciting it?
cards.back: Interpretation guides appropriate stress, pace, tone and pauses.

topics.subject: re
topics.title: Eucharist, miracles & evaluating sources

notes.heading: State the Catholic teaching accurately
notes.body: In Catholic teaching the Eucharist involves Christ’s real presence. Transubstantiation describes a change of substance while the appearances of bread and wine remain. A report of an extraordinary visible event is therefore different from the sacramental teaching itself. Present a belief as Catholic teaching, and a reported event as a claim to investigate.

notes.heading: Keep an observation separate from its interpretation
notes.body: For the Classroom research task, distinguish the account of an event, the people or institutions investigating it, the reported findings and the interpretation attached to them. A statement on a popular webpage is not automatically the original scientific report. Record exactly what each source supports and what it does not establish.

notes.heading: Build a traceable research record
notes.body: For one chosen event, record the place, date, source author, publication date, investigation details and relevant limitations. Compare sources, cite the original report where available, and explain religious relevance in your own reasoned words. Do not invent a named investigator, tissue finding or Church judgement when your sources do not verify it.

practice.question: Distinguish the Eucharist’s Catholic sacramental teaching from a reported Eucharistic miracle.
practice.answer: The sacramental teaching concerns Christ’s real presence and transubstantiation. A reported miracle describes an extraordinary claimed event requiring its own historical and evidential examination. The two are not interchangeable.

practice.question: A website says “scientists proved it” but names no researchers or report. What information should a research note seek?
practice.answer: Named investigators or institutions, the original report, dates, methods, the material examined, results and limitations. The phrase alone does not allow readers to trace or evaluate the evidence.

practice.question: What belongs in a bibliography entry for a webpage?
practice.answer: At minimum, the available author or responsible organisation, page title, publication/update date where stated, URL and access date, using the teacher’s required citation style.

practice.question: Why should you distinguish the date of an event from the date of its investigation?
practice.answer: They describe different stages in the evidence chain. A later investigation does not automatically supply direct evidence for every detail reported about an earlier event.

practice.question: Give a respectful way to distinguish belief from a test result in writing.
practice.answer: For example: “Catholics may interpret the reported event in relation to Eucharistic belief; the report’s stated observation is …”. Complete the observation only with a finding your source actually documents.

practice.question: Why should the religious-relevance section do more than repeat the event’s description?
practice.answer: It asks for an explained connection to Catholic belief or practice and a motivated evaluation. Retelling the event does not by itself show its relevance or support a personal conclusion.

challenges.question: A report establishes that a sample contains human tissue. Does that observation alone establish every historical and theological claim made about the sample? Explain.
challenges.answer: No. Identify exactly what the test establishes, how the sample was obtained and authenticated, and what other claims require separate evidence. A measured observation, a historical account and a theological interpretation are different kinds of claims.

challenges.question: Two webpages repeat the same story word for word. Why is this not necessarily independent corroboration?
challenges.answer: They may both copy one earlier account. Trace their sources and assess the original evidence rather than counting repeated webpages as separate investigations. Independent corroboration requires evidence not merely repeated wording.

topics.subject: re
topics.title: Saints, virtue & reflective research

notes.heading: Connect a virtue with an action
notes.body: The Saint Project asks for a biography and an explanation of admired qualities. A virtue is more than a flattering label: explain the concrete action, the difficulty involved and the quality the action illustrates. Catholic recognition of a saint concerns a life of holiness; distinguish the historical evidence about a person from your interpretation of their example.

notes.heading: Organise biography as a meaningful sequence
notes.body: Record dates and places, family circumstances, occupation, significant events and the circumstances of death using reliable sources. Select details that help explain the person’s choices. Verify a quotation’s wording and attribution before using it; an attractive quotation found online is not proof that the person said it.

notes.heading: Make reflection practical and specific
notes.body: The teacher’s brief also asks for qualities you aspire to and concrete ways to develop them. Connect an admired action with a realistic action in your own context. Explain why you selected the person, give credit for images and information, and prepare to answer questions rather than simply reading a list of facts.

practice.question: Turn “the saint was generous” into a research question that could support an explanation.
practice.answer: Ask what the person gave or did, for whom, at what cost or difficulty, and which sources document it. Those details can support a reasoned account of generosity.

practice.question: Why is a date-and-place timeline useful before drafting a biography?
practice.answer: It checks sequence, helps identify contradictions and places significant choices in context. It supports a coherent account rather than an unordered list of facts.

practice.question: Give a concrete application of the quality “service” in a school context.
practice.answer: For example, commit to a specific regular task that meets a real need, such as helping maintain a class resource collection, and reflect on whether it helps others. The example should be practical rather than a vague promise to be better.

practice.question: A quotation appears on several unattributed image cards. What should you check before presenting it?
practice.answer: Find a reliable attribution to the person or an original work, verify the wording and context, and cite it. If it cannot be verified, do not present it as an authenticated quotation.

practice.question: Why should a presentation include reasons for choosing the saint?
practice.answer: The task includes personal reflection: explain which documented qualities matter to you and how the example connects to your own aims, rather than relying only on fame or an attractive image.

practice.question: How can an image support a presentation rather than decorate it?
practice.answer: Use an image that helps explain the person, setting or point being discussed, identify what it shows and credit its source. Visuals should contribute to understanding.

challenges.question: Can a biography be factually detailed yet weak at explaining virtue? Explain the missing link.
challenges.answer: Yes. Dates and events establish information, but an explanation of virtue must connect particular choices and circumstances to a quality and justify that interpretation. The task requires both knowledge and reflection.

challenges.question: Two sources disagree about a saint’s early life. Why should a researcher report the uncertainty instead of combining both accounts into one confident story?
challenges.answer: Combining incompatible claims can manufacture an account that no source supports. Compare dates, provenance and evidence, explain the disagreement and qualify the conclusion where verification is not possible.
